title: What did India's Sun telescope see during a giant solar flare?
blurb: Aditya-L1's ultraviolet camera caught a huge flare on 22 February 2024, in colours of light where no one had pictured a flare up close before.

original.title: Near- and Mid-ultraviolet Observations of X-6.3 Flare on 2024 February 22 Recorded by the Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope on board Aditya-L1
original.authors: Soumya Roy, Durgesh Tripathi, Sreejith Padinhatteeri, A. N. Ramaprakash, Abhilash R. Sarwade and others

cards.b: The Sun sometimes throws out a sudden, huge burst of energy called a solar flare. Scientists mostly study flares in X-rays, a kind of light our eyes cannot see. Very few have seen a flare close up in ultraviolet, which is light just beyond the violet of a rainbow. Our eyes cannot see that either. So what does a big flare look like in ultraviolet?

India sent a telescope called Aditya-L1 to watch the Sun. It was launched on 2 September 2023. One of its cameras is SUIT, the Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope, which takes pictures of the Sun in ultraviolet light. Soumya Roy and Durgesh Tripathi, at an astronomy institute in Pune called IUCAA, studied SUIT's pictures with scientists from ISRO, IISER Kolkata, Manipal and other places. They published in 2025.

SUIT has 11 filters. A filter is a piece of glass that lets through only some of the light. Eight of SUIT's filters are narrow, and each lets through one thin slice of ultraviolet. On 22 February 2024, a very strong flare burst out near a dark patch on the Sun. Scientists call it X6.3, where X means the strongest class of flare. SUIT photographed it through its 8 narrow filters about once a minute. The team compared the pictures with data from other telescopes.

img.alt: Eight small ultraviolet pictures of the same flare, one for each SUIT filter, each in a different false colour
img.credit: Figure 2, Roy, Tripathi and others, The Astrophysical Journal Letters (2025), CC BY 4.0

cards.b: The flare showed up in all 8 filters. In four of them, it was brightest at the very moment its X-rays were strongest. In two, it was brightest about 2 minutes later. In the last two, it peaked later still. In one filter they saw kernels, small very bright spots inside the flare, for the first time. For four of the colours, it was also the first close look at a flare.

img.alt: The flare region in eight ultraviolet colours, with black arrows pointing to two small bright kernels
img.credit: Figure 1b to 1i, Roy, Tripathi and others, The Astrophysical Journal Letters (2025), CC BY 4.0

cards.b: This is one flare, the first big flare SUIT saw on the face of the Sun. Many other instruments agreed with SUIT about when the flare was strongest, which makes the results stronger. Some questions are still open. Why do the colours peak at different times? What makes the kernels? Answering these will take many more flares.

A flare suddenly heats the layers of the Sun's air. Scientists still argue about where some of a flare's light comes from, and each new colour is a new clue. SUIT keeps watching the Sun, so it will catch many more flares. This study shows what the telescope can do.

Find the edge of the rainbow. Fill a clear tumbler with water and put it on a sunny windowsill, with white paper on the floor below. Move the paper until you see a little rainbow. The water bends the sunlight and splits it into its colours. Which colour is at each end? Violet is at one end. Just past it is ultraviolet, the light SUIT sees. You cannot see it, which is why SUIT needs a special camera.

SUIT's eight filters show the same flare a little differently. Which picture shows the real flare? Or are they all real, each showing one part of the truth? Can you think of something at home that looks different in different light?
